task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-11-01, in the area of player absence and offensive reorganization):
The teammate with the closest pre-absence initiation profile (or most minutes / initiations / same-position minutes) is the largest gainer in the absent player's primary types.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=148; 148 spells; 11 cases

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: teammate replacement gain in absent player's primary play types
absorption vs cascade of play-type usage during absence
methodological_questions: How to define the 'closest' pre-absence initiation profile (cosine similarity, minutes, initiations, same-position minutes)?
How to define the 'primary types' of the absent player (top-k play types by initiation share, above threshold)?
How to define and measure 'gain' in those play types for each teammate (absolute increase, relative increase)?
How to control for game context, opponent, and coaching decisions that could confound teammate usage?
What is the required sample size (number of absence spells) to detect a meaningful effect given the small available n=148 spells / 11 cases?
How to handle multiple testing across different similarity definitions and across spells?

historical_evidence.finding: mean sim ABSORBED +0.863 vs CASCADE +0.848; Spearman(sim, -gap)=-0.19 (wrong-signed). Embiid 23-24 cascades with Reed sim 0.94. Verdict: null; adequately powered null result; similarity does not separate absorption from cascade.

[[prior work]] median self_sim=+0.129 decoy_sim=+0.049; T1 median Delta=+0.0557 perm_p=0.0050; 173/294=0.5884 sign_test_p=2.872e-03. A mover's displacement signature is more similar across franchises than profile-matched destination decoys.

Connector absence displaces team offensive identity (D_A) more than usage-matched non-organizer absence. Unmatched: conn vs role D_A 0.2020 vs 0.1021, t=5.97 p=2.87e-08. Usage-matched vs role: paired dD_A +0.1151, P(conn>ctrl)=81.2%, t=6.35 p=7.35e-09 n=96.
Real on/off absence of a shaper displaces the team fingerprint more than a usage-matched non-shaper: Delta D_A=+0.115, t=6.35, p~7e-9, shaper larger in 81% of pairs; n=908, 96 matched pairs.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using play-type replacement similarity (initiation profile similarity) to separate absorption from cascade during player absence
failed_approaches.why: Adequately powered null result: similarity does not separate absorption from cascade (Spearman r=-0.19, wrong-signed); almost always findable. Risk of label/classification error ([prior work]).

evidence_establishes: Earlier work ([prior work][prior work]) tested the hypothesis that having a similar-profile teammate separates cases where the absent player's play types are absorbed by one teammate from cases where they cascade across multiple teammates; it found a null result (similarity not predictive). This is the most directly relevant prior evidence.

Shaper/connector absences cause larger team offensive identity displacement than usage-matched non-organizer absences (SF-[prior work], SF-[prior work]), but that evidence concerns overall team fingerprint change, not which specific teammate gains the missing player's primary types.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether the teammate with the closest pre-absence initiation profile is the largest individual gainer in the absent player's primary play types (the precise research question).
Whether alternative operationalizations of similarity (minutes, initiations, same-position minutes) predict who gains the most.
Whether the finding generalizes to the specific 11-case sample available in the current data window.
own_inferences: The null result from SF-[prior work] on similarity and absorption/cascade strongly suggests that pre-absence initiation-profile similarity will not successfully predict which teammate gains the missing player's primary types; any test run on the current data is likely to yield a null or inconclusive result.

The sample size reported for the current project (n=148 spells, but only 11 cases) is far too small to detect a realistic effect even if one existed; SF-[prior work] used ~23 absences and was judged adequately powered for a null result, so 11 cases would be underpowered for any meaningful inference.
Confounding by coaching strategy, opponent adjustments, and game situation is very difficult to disentangle without a larger sample and careful controls.
uncertainties: The exact definitions of 'closest pre-absence initiation profile' and 'largest gainer in primary types' may yield different outcomes, but these definitions cannot be fully settled without exploratory analysis that is precluded by the small sample.
It is possible that a more refined similarity metric or play-type definition could produce a different result, but the prior null on similarity suggests this is unlikely.
The number 11 cases is recorded but its meaning is not fully specified; if it refers to absence spells meeting some quality threshold, it is still too small.

historical_effect.explanation: Prior work ([prior work][prior work]) directly tested the role of similarity in determining absorption versus cascade and found an adequately powered null result. Without that evidence, one might have considered proceeding with a careful study given the apparent plausibility of the hypothesis. However, the combination of a clean null on a closely related hypothesis and the extraordinarily small current sample (11 cases) changes the decision from 'maybe proceed with caution' to a clear 'do not proceed'.

blocking_constraints.text: Only 11 cases available, far below the minimum needed (estimated >100 spells) to detect a plausible effect size; any test would be severely underpowered.
The pool of absence spells in the data is small, and many spells may lack a clear 'closest' teammate or sufficient pre-absence initiation data to compute profiles reliably.
Initiation profile similarity metrics may be unstable for players with low volume of initiations, and 'largest gainer' may be determined by a handful of possessions.

prior_work.summary: Study family SF-[prior work] tested a closely related hypothesis (similar-profile teammate separates absorption from cascade) and obtained an adequately powered null result. This does not test the exact current question (that the closest-profile teammate is the largest gainer in the absent player's primary types) but renders it highly unlikely.

risks.text: Only 11 cases; far too few for adequately powered inference on a continuous gain measure.
Even the 148 spells may include many with insufficient pre-absence data or unclear replacement structure.
Initiation profiles are estimated with noise; similarity scores may be unstable; 'primary types' and 'largest gainer' are subject to small-sample variation in play-type counts.
Coaching decisions, opponent matchups, and game context can determine which teammate's usage increases, confounding the relationship between pre-absence similarity and post-absence gain.
Play-type labels assigned by the inferrer may contain classification errors, which can affect both similarity computation and gain measurement.
Multiple similarity definitions (profile, minutes, initiations, same-position) and multiple spells demand correction for multiplicity that would further erode power.

design.estimand: The difference between the gain (increase from pre-absence to during-absence period) in the absent player's primary play-type shares for the teammate with the closest pre-absence initiation profile and the average gain of all other teammates.
design.unit: One player absence spell that meets inclusion criteria (e.g., at least 8 consecutive games missed, sufficient pre-absence initiation data for all rotation teammates).
design.sample: All absence spells from the 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular seasons that have complete play-by-play and initiation data, excluding garbage-time possessions. Minimum required sample: >100 spells (current data: ~11 candidate spells is insufficient).
design.power: Simulation-based power analysis using a one-sample t-test of the most-similar teammate's gain minus average others' gain; target 80% power for a Cohen's d of 0.3 with alpha=0.05 (one-sided) requires approximately 100 spells with adequate variability; unavailable.
design.controls: Fixed effects for team and season; controls for opponent defensive rating, home/away, and number of other absent players.
design.falsification: Replace the most-similar teammate with a randomly chosen non-teammate from the same roster and test whether the 'gain' difference persists; also test whether the metric predicts gain for play types that were not primary for the absent player (should not).
design.multiplicity: Pre-register a single primary similarity metric (e.g., cosine similarity of play-type initiation shares, regularized to handle zero counts); if multiple metrics are explored, apply Bonferroni correction and report all.
design.decision_rule: One-sided paired t-test (or Wilcoxon) that the most-similar teammate's gain exceeds the mean gain of other teammates, at alpha=0.025. Null rejection requires survival of multiplicity correction and passes falsification checks.
design.data_version: Snapshot as of 2026-11-01, codebase tagged and archived.
